info.bio: Sus 50 años de vida artística han convertido a los Drifters en algo más que un clásico del Soul, pudiéndose afirmar con toda propiedad que son toda una institución de la música. Su larga lista de miembros en tan dilatada trayectoria incluyen algunos de los vocalistas más grandes de la historia del R&B, como Clyde Mc Phatter, su fundador, Ben E. King, Rudy Lewis o Johnny Moore. Este recopilatorio presenta los grandes hits de sus voces doradas

scenes.name: El soul conquista Gran Bretaña
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: El 26 de octubre «Reach Out I’ll Be There» de los Four Tops, con la flauta de aire oriental, el fraseo dylaniano de Lamont Dozier y la interpretación de su vida de Levi Stubbs, desbancó a «Distant Drums» y fue número 1: el momento en que la música negra americana ocupó el centro de la cultura juvenil británica, al revés que en el boom del beat. Lo habían preparado durante años los entusiastas: Dave Godin, que fundó en 1963 la Tamla Motown Appreciation Society, viajó a Detroit, llevó «Where Did Our Love Go» a los piratas y bautizó el sello Tamla Motown (marzo de 1965, con una gira de la revista que fracasó fuera de Londres); Guy Stevens, que pinchaba discos negros en el Scene y dirigió Sue Records para Chris Blackwell; Roger Eagle en el Twisted Wheel de Mánchester; Tony Hall promocionando Atlantic («In the Midnight Hour», el «My Girl» de Otis Redding); el DJ Jeff Dexter mezclando soul y ska en Tiles, el club subterráneo de Oxford Street del mod de masas que visitó Tom Wolfe. En otoño de 1966 Atlantic y Motown copaban las listas; Otis Redding metió a 8.000 personas en Tiles; los Four Tops arrasaron en el Savile de Brian Epstein el 13 de noviembre. El racismo, aun así, seguía ahí.

scenes.name: Antes del diluvio
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La «edad oscura» del rock'n'roll: los rebeldes son sustituidos por ídolos adolescentes educados y el Brill Building devuelve el poder a los compositores profesionales. Pero en esos años se incuban la revolución futura: la guitarra fuzz de Link Wray, los bailes de moda (el twist), el rock instrumental de guitarras (Duane Eddy, Ventures, Shadows), el calipso y el primer ska, el doo-wop más inventivo (Coasters, Drifters, Five Royales), el nacimiento del soul (Sam Cooke, Ray Charles, Motown, Stax), el estudio como instrumento de Joe Meek y el surf de los Beach Boys y del «muro de sonido» de Phil Spector.

podcast.title: Leiber and Stoller's Post-Elvis Work (Post-1958)
podcast.body: After their definitive professional break with Elvis and subsequent loss of jobs at RCA, The Drifters were another R&B group that Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller focused their songwriting talents on. "The Drifters."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 72: "Trouble" by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: Rudy Lewis's Sudden Death (May 21, 1964)
podcast.body: Tragedy struck on May 21, 1964, when Rudy Lewis died suddenly. Johnny Moore was informed of the news by Sylvia Van Topoe of Mickey and Sylvia. Despite the devastating news, the group proceeded to the studio to record as scheduled, including songs like "I Don't Want to Go On Without You." "Trashety struck on the day the drifters recorded what would be their last US top 10 hit, the 21st of May 1964."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: George Treadwell's Death and Faye Treadwell's Takeover (1967)
podcast.body: George Treadwell, the Drifters' manager, died in 1967. His wife, Faye Treadwell, subsequently took over the management of the group. This change marked a significant shift in the group's history and led to further personnel changes and internal disputes. "There were several more line-up changes, but the big change came in 1967 when George Treadwell died."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: End of Atlantic Records Career (1970)
podcast.body: By 1970, after numerous lineup changes, squabbles, and splinter groups, the Drifters' career with Atlantic Records came to an end. "And by 1970 the Drifter's career on Atlantic was over."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: Al's Baby Hubbed Drafted
podcast.body: Al's Baby Hubbed, the group's bass singer, was drafted, leading to further lineup instability as the group went through several singers before settling on Tommy Evans, who had previous experience with earlier Drifters lineups. "And then Al's Baby Hubbed, the group's bass singer, was drafted, and the group got in a couple of different singers before settling on Tommy Evans."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: Benny King's Departure
podcast.body: After "Save the Last Dance for Me" became a number one hit and King's last single with the group, his manager Lover Patterson reached an agreement with Drifters manager George Treadwell, allowing King to transition smoothly into a solo career. There were also reports of King Records negotiating to buy the Drifters' contract from Atlantic. "After King's manager Lover Patterson came to an agreement with the drifters manager George Treadwell, the woodluck King moves smoothly into a solo career."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: Charlie Thomas's Departure (After 9 Years)
podcast.body: Shortly after Faye Treadwell took over management in 1967, Charlie Thomas, who had been in the group for the longest continuous period (nine years at that point), decided to leave, contributing to further lineup instability and the eventual splintering of the group. "And shortly after that, Charlie Thomas, the person who had been in the group for the longest continuous time, nine years at that point, decided to leave."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: Charlie Thomas's Drifters (USA)
podcast.body: This version consisted of Doc Green, Charlie Thomas, and Del's Bayri Hubs, members from Benny King's era of the group. Charlie Thomas won the legal right to use the Drifters name in the USA in 1972 and continues to tour with his own group, though no other members from that specific lineup are still with him. "Then there was a version of the Drifters that consisted of Doc Green, Charlie Thomas and Del's Bayri Hubs, the people who had been in Benny King's version of the group."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: Current UK Drifters Lineup
podcast.body: The current UK version of The Drifters is managed by George and Faye Treadwell's daughter and does not include any members who were part of the group before 2010. Despite the lack of original members, they continue to fill medium-sized theaters on national tours, as audiences prioritize hearing the classic songs. "The current UK version of the Drifters has nobody who was in the group before 2010, and is managed by George and Fay Treadwell's daughter."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: End of US Top 10 Success
podcast.body: After "Under the Boardwalk" reached number 4, the Drifters had no more top 10 hits in the US, with their best subsequent chart performance being "Saturday Night at the Movies" which scraped the top 20. "But after under the boardwalk, which went to number 4, they had no more top 10 hits in the US."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: George Treadwell's Insurance Plan
podcast.body: Aware of Rudy Lewis's potential solo departure, manager George Treadwell brought back Johnny Moore, who had been in the group in the 1950s and had recently left The Drapers, to trade off lead vocals with Lewis in the studio for several months as a contingency. "So he got Johnny Moore, who had been in the group in the 50s and had just left the drapers to join, and for a few months Lewis and Moore traded off leads in the studio."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: Group Identity Bigger Than Members
podcast.body: The Drifters are cited as a unique case where the group's identity was genuinely bigger than its members, allowing them to continue making exceptional records regardless of who was involved. "It's the only case I know where a group identity was genuinely bigger than the members, where whoever was involved somehow they carried on making exceptional records."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: Inspiration for Stop-Time Section
podcast.body: Their song, released a few months before "Only the Lonely," utilized strings and rhythmic disorientation in a similar way. This may have inspired the eight-bar stop-time section in "Only the Lonely," which stood out as a straightforward part within the song's otherwise bizarre structure. "The only incongruity there is a very minor one. A brief move to the fifth chord, which is the kind of extremely minor deviation from the key that's par for the course in pop music."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 83: "Only the Lonely" by Roy Orbison

podcast.title: James Poindexter and Stage Fright
podcast.body: James Poindexter was brought in as a replacement for Johnny Lee Williams but suffered from stage fright, leading the group to perform as a trio for several months before Rudy Lewis joined as the new lead singer. "The drifters got in a replacement for Williams, James Pointexter, but he turned out to have stage fright, and the group spent several months as a trio."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: Johnny Lee Williams' Departure (Mobile, Alabama)
podcast.body: During a tour, Johnny Lee Williams decided to leave the Drifters in Mobile, Alabama, expressing dissatisfaction with not getting to sing lead vocals. He was originally from Mobile. His departure necessitated finding a new replacement. "When they were on tour and got to Mobile, Alabama, Johnny Lee Williams said that he was just going to stay there and not continue on the tour."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: Johnny Moore's Significance (UK Drifters)
podcast.body: Johnny Moore served as the lead singer for the UK version of The Drifters until his death in 1998. His long tenure and prior involvement with hits in the 1950s and 1960s meant that approximately 80% of all records released under the Drifters name featured his vocals, making his group considered a "real version" of the Drifters. "Roughly 80% of records released as by the Drifters had had more singing on them."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: Legal Problems and King's Contract (Pre-solo)
podcast.body: The Drifters faced legal issues when contracts for individual members were sold to George Tradwell, owner of the Drifters name. Benny King's contract was not included in this sale, leading to an unusual situation where King sang lead on studio records but was not allowed to tour with the group, necessitating a soundalike singer for live performances. "When the contracts for the individual members had been sold to George Tradwell, the owner of the drifters name, Benny King's contract had not been sold with the rest."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: Lieber & Stoller Collaboration
podcast.body: The Drifters were among the "black performers" whom Jerry Lieber and Mike Stoller admired and recorded with almost exclusively for Atlantic Records. "And at the same time, they were also attached to Atlantic, where they were recording almost exclusively with the black performers that they admired, such as Ruth Brown, LeVern Baker and The Drifters."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 68: "Yakety Yak" by the Coasters

podcast.title: Longest Lasting Lineup Under Treadwell (Post-Lewis)
podcast.body: The lineup of Johnny Moore, Charlie Thomas, Gene Pearson, and Johnny Terry was the longest lasting of all the versions of the group managed by George Treadwell, remaining together for two years, following the success of "Under the Boardwalk." "This version of the group, Johnny Moore, Charlie Thomas, Jean Pearson and Johnny Terry, would be the longest lasting of all the versions of the group managed by George Treadwell, staying together for two years."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: Post-Johnny Moore Confusion and Lawsuits
podcast.body: After Johnny Moore's death in 1998, the situation surrounding The Drifters became very confusing, involving the Treadwell family reportedly abandoning and then reclaiming the trademark, leading to a series of lawsuits. "But after Moor's death, it gets very confusing."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: Post-King Personnel Shifts
podcast.body: After Benny King's departure, Atlantic Records began releasing material from their vault, including songs with King's leads and older records. The group then experienced further significant personnel changes. "After King left, Atlantic started releasing whatever material they had in their vault, both songs with King's Leeds and older records from the earlier lineup of drifters."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: Rudy Lewis's Solo Aspirations and Death
podcast.body: Rudy Lewis, who had been the lead singer since shortly after King's departure, considered a solo career and even released an unsuccessful solo single. Tragically, he died suddenly on May 21, 1964, the same day the Drifters were scheduled to record their last US top 10 hit. "But Rudy Lewis, the lead singer of the group since just after King had left, was thinking of going solo and even released one solo single."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: Studio vs. Touring Lineup (Pre-solo)
podcast.body: Due to Benny King's contract not being sold with the rest of the group, there were five Drifters in the studio (including King) but only four in the touring group, with Johnny Lee Williams singing King's parts on stage. This "unworkable arrangement" was surprisingly successful initially. "So there were now five drifters in the studio, but only four of them in the touring group."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: The Original Drifters (Bill Pinkney)
podcast.body: This version formed in 1958 after the first set of Drifters was fired. It was originally made up of members from the early 1950s lineups and evolved into a revolving door group based around Bill Pinkney, the bass singer from the Clyde McFrattle lineup, operating until Pinkney's death in 2007. "There was a group called, The Original Drifters, which had formed in 1958 after the first set of Drifters had been fired, and was originally made up entirely of members of the early 50s line-ups, but which was now a revolving dog group based around Bill Pinkney, the bass singer of the Clyde McFrattle lineup, and stayed that way until Pinkney's death in 2007."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: Three Versions of The Drifters (1970s)
podcast.body: By 1970, three distinct versions of The Drifters existed: "The Original Drifters" centered around Bill Pinkney, a group led by Charlie Thomas that eventually won the right to use the name in the USA, and a UK-based group managed by Faye Treadwell with Johnny Moore as lead singer. "By this point there were three different versions of the Drifters."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: Total Members on Atlantic (34 individuals)
podcast.body: During their tenure with Atlantic Records, a total of 34 different individuals were members of The Drifters, illustrating a highly fluid lineup where the group's identity often superseded its individual members. "In total 34 different people were members of the Drifters during their time with Atlantic records."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King

podcast.title: UK-Based Drifters (Faye Treadwell & Johnny Moore)
podcast.body: Managed by Faye Treadwell with Johnny Moore as lead singer, this group moved to the UK in 1972 and scored significant hits with re-releases of mid-1960s records that had originally been flops, such as "Saturday Night at the Movies," "At the Club," and "Come On Over to My Place," all making the UK top 10. They subsequently had nine more UK top 10 hits with new material between 1973 and 1976. "Then there was a UK-based group, managed by Fade Redwell, with Johnny Moorvers lead singer."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 94: "Stand By Me", by Ben E. King
